data.text/markdown: Data Preprocessing

In this notebook we prepare the data for further experiments. The data that we have is raw data obtained using Alpaca. When fetching, we tried to get as much data as possible for the given assets, without getting into the COVID-19 range, as this period was very unpredictable. It might be interesting to include it later, to check how our methods work across market regimes.
Alpaca returns more columns that we will actually need, thus we first load the datasets from corresponding Parquet files and drop the unneccessary columns.

To make proper validation of the dataset easier we will now convert the timestamps from UTC to local NYC time. This will also make filtering of the dataset simpler, since similarly to Teller we will not be considering overnight returns. Following that we filter out any bars that are not inside the trading session. Any bar starting at 16:00 is also dropped. Notice that the timestamp of a given bar means the time it has opened.

data.text/markdown: After this initial preprocessing we can create data quality reports for the datasets. In particular we want to inspect coverage rate for each asset and find out the exact time range of the available data. The missing bars will be aggregated over trading sessions and 5 minute intervals. Afterwards, we will try to find out how many 5 minute returns we will be able to actually compute without imputing any data. This amount may be different across assets.

data.text/markdown: At first glance our data looks solid and seems to have good coverage for almost all assets. The most worrying are our target datasets, who seem to have proportionally the most missing data. This is problematic, because data related to those assets is already quite limited. Now, we will inspect those missing candles in detail across assets. We want to find out how many 5-minute returns are impossible to compute. Only after that we will make decisions regarding imputing or dropping parts of the dataset.

We now compute all the possible log returns over 5 minute intervals. Below we can see how many missing values there is per asset per trading session. As expected before the most troubling ones are the missing returns of target assets.

data.text/markdown: For our HAR model we want to use 22 day rolling volatility as feature. Let's see how many of those windows we lose due to missing values.

As we can see the returns for some of the assets are completely unusable. In particular, for "CHWY" we wouldn't be able to construct a single 22 day rolling volatility value. For a lot of the assets, we have a decent coverage. Regardless of that, we will now precisely inspect source of those missing 5 minute returns and try to compute them again in a less strict way, which unfortunately may decrease the reliability of our data, but it's not possible to proceed any further without doing that. We start by inspecting for each asset the source of missing 5-minute returns. Since for computing the returns within an interval we don't need its insides, we only have to check how many NaN's are caused by missing start of the interval and how many are caused by missing the end of the interval.

data.text/markdown: One can notice that because of the method of computing the returns, imputing some of the missing_end's would have a great effect on missing_returns_5m. It might be reasonable to fill some of the missing prices using the closest previous price. However, we shouldn't just use any closest available price from past, as this may lead to huge errors if we sample from very far away. For that reason, we first inspect asset by asset how many of the missing_end values can be filled by going back in time by 1, 2 or 3 minutes and how many don't have any previous price available.

MSFT: 2016-02-02 - two bars(lag2 and lag7 consecutive), 2016-02-22: about 60 minute missing block, 2018-05-02, 2018-05-03 missing almost entirely CSCO: same as above AMZN: same as above + some lag1 and very few lag2 EBAY: same as AMZN WMT: 2016-02-02 same as above, 2019-08-12 missing 30minutes block, very few lag1 COST: 2016-02-02 as above, 2018-05-02, 2018-05-03 missing entirely pretty much JPM: 2016-02-02 as above, 2019-08-12 as WMT BAC: 2016-02-02 as above, 2019-08-12 lag2 lag7, then lag3 and lag8 JNJ: 2016-02-02 as above, 2019-08-12 as WMT, 2019-10-29 missing ~30 minutes at the end PFE: 2016-02-02 as above, 2019-08-12 as WMT, 2019-10-09 missing about an hour straight then lag5 and lag4 at the same day XOM: 2016-02-02 as above, 2019-08-12 as WMT CVX: 2016-02-02 as above, 2019-08-12 as WMT CRWD: 2019-06-12 (ipo) a bunch of NaN at the start some lag1 lag2 very few lag3 lag4 CHWY: similar to above when it comes to NaNs, some lag1 lag2 and lag3 and lag4 but not much, 2019-08-12 some missing up to lag15

Through a manual inspection of the above table we are able to see that there are maybe 4 problematic days with a lot of missing data. Other missing endpoints are can be filled using previous candles or the ones before and since there is not that many of them in total, it filling them using past data shouldn't make the data too unreliable. So for now we will fill the 'easy' ones and re-run the diagnostics to see what else can we do.
